title: GPU fleet capacity + IaC & CI/CD integrated guide
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Purpose

This page consolidates the operational and engineering guidance for Redwood's GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform / IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines. It is intended for infrastructure engineers, SREs, and platform owners who implement, operate, and troubleshoot inference capacity in hosted and dedicated environments.

Scope

- GPU fleet provisioning and node pool design (AWS/GCP/Azure patterns)
- Capacity planning targets and SLOs for throughput and headroom
- Terraform modules and IaC patterns used by infra teams
- CI/CD pipelines for module & service delivery (Terraform, Packer, container builds)
- Runbook entries for common operational incidents and escalations
- Networking and cloud account configuration guardrails

Quick summary (TL;DR)

- Target average utilization: 55-70% GPU utilization per node for cost-efficiency, with 20-30% headroom for burst traffic.
- Autoscale policy: scale-up when 10m avg queued requests > 25 and avg GPU utilization > 65%; scale-down after 15m sustained utilization < 30% and no queue.
- Terraform modules: use module/gpu-node-pool (v2.3+) and module/vpc-standard (v1.4+). All changes require a plan review + two approvers for production.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions + Atlantis for IaC; build pipeline runs unit tests, lint, terraform plan in PR; apply gated to protected branches with manual approval.

Ownership and contacts

- GPU fleet owner: infra-capacity@redwood.com (primary: Aisha Patel)
- IaC & Terraform modules: infra-iac@redwood.com (primary: Leo Martinez)
- CI/CD & release pipelines: infra-ci@redwood.com (primary: Sofia Chen)
- Oncall rota: see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/oncall-rotations

Operational SLOs and KPIs

- Availability (node-level): 99.95% (measured as node readiness for production clusters)
- Latency SLO (API tail p99): 600ms for short requests, 2s for multi-token generation workloads in dedicated clusters (customer SLAs may be stricter)
- Capacity headroom: maintain >= 20% free GPU cycles across the fleet under normal traffic
- Time-to-scale: new capacity should be available and scheduling within 5 minutes after scale-up trigger in the majority of events
- Incident classification thresholds:
  - P1: sustained cluster saturation (>95% GPU usage or >90% pod scheduling failure) for >5 minutes
  - P2: partial degradation (slot queueing or increased 95th latency) for >10 minutes

Node pool design patterns

- Homogeneous pools per hardware class: group nodes by GPU type (e.g. A100-40GB, H100-80GB, T4) and by tenancy (shared-hosted vs dedicated-customer).
- Mixed-instance scaling: use heterogeneous instance sizes only for flexible non-latency-sensitive workloads; prefer uniform instance types for strict latency SLOs.
- Storage and local NVMe: attach ephemeral NVMe for large-model KV caches; keep model artifacts on S3/GCS and mount via init containers.
- Node labels & taints:
  - label: inference.gpu.type = a100-40
  - taint: dedicated=true:NoSchedule for customer-dedicated pools

Terraform / IaC modules (patterns and examples)

- Module naming: module/gpu-node-pool, module/vpc-standard, module/iam-service-accounts, module/route53-privatedns.
- Version pinning: all module references must pin to a semver tag. Avoid floating `main`.
- Example module usage (short):

  module "gpu_node_pool" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v2.3.1"
    name_prefix = "inference-a100"
    gpu_type = "a100-40gb"
    min_size = 2
    max_size = 50
    autoscaling = true
    labels = { "team" = "inference", "env" = var.env }
  }

- Recommended variables: cluster_name, env, region, gpu_type, min_size, max_size, node_taint, gpu_driver_version.
- IAM/service accounts: use least-privilege roles; attach instance profile with limited S3/GCS and metrics permissions.
- State management: remote state stored in encrypted S3/GCS with state locking (DynamoDB/Cloud KMS).

Terraform CI/CD & PR workflow

- Local dev checklist:
  1. tflint --init && tflint
  2. terraform fmt -check
  3. terraform validate -no-color

- PR checks (GitHub Actions + Atlantis):
  - On PR: run tflint, terraform fmt, terraform init && terraform plan (using mock credentials).
  - Plan output posts as comment in PR.
  - Tag PR with `infra/plan-ok` when plan reviewed.
  - Apply gated to protected branches (e.g. `prod`, `stage`) via Atlantis or a manual approver flow requiring two approvers.

- Secrets and credentials: use GitHub Actions OIDC + cloud provider role assumption. Do not store long-lived keys in repositories.

CI/CD for runtime (containers and model-serving code)

- Pipeline steps (high level):
  1. Build: container image build using BuildKit, multi-arch where required
  2. Static checks: linters, go vet / python lint, license checks
  3. Unit tests and small e2e smoke tests (local inference with tiny model)
  4. Image push to ECR/GCR (immutable tag: git sha + semver)
  5. Canary deploy: automated canary to 5% of traffic with smoke tests and metrics validation
  6. Gradual rollout to 100% or rollback on failure criteria

- Canary validation criteria:
  - No increase in 5xx errors > 0.5% relative to baseline
  - Latency p95 not worse than +15% vs baseline
  - Successful model correctness smoke tests (predefined prompts)

Autoscaling and scheduler behavior

- Kubernetes cluster-autoscaler patterns: use Cluster-Autoscaler with custom metrics hook for queued requests. For more deterministic behavior, use a control-plane autoscaler service that watches a queue-length metric and triggers node pool scale events through the Terraform API or cloud provider API (only for dedicated pools).
- Scheduler preemption: prefer bin-packing for inference containers; reserve CPU for system daemons.
- Batching pods: prefer a sidecar that reports backlog length; autoscaler uses backlog + target utilization to compute required replica and node counts.

Metrics and dashboards (owner: infra-monitoring)

- Key metrics to surface:
  - cluster_gpu_utilization_percent (per-pool)
  - inference_pod_queue_length (histogram)
  - pod_scheduling_failures (count)
  - node_boot_time_seconds (p95/99)
  - instance_replacement_rate (per-day)
  - terraform_apply_failures (count)

- Dashboards: GPU Fleet Overview, Per-Pool Capacity, Scheduling Failures, Autoscaler Decisions. Alerting thresholds:
  - P1 alert: cluster_gpu_utilization_percent > 90% for 5m OR pod_scheduling_failures > 10/min sustained 5m
  - P2 alert: inference_pod_queue_length > 50 for 10m

Runbook: high level incident flow (common scenarios)

1) P1 - Cluster saturation / scheduling failures\   - Pager to infra-oncall. Immediately run:
     - kubectl get pods -n inference --field-selector=status.phase!=Running -o wide
     - kubectl top nodes | sort -k3 -nr
     - Check autoscaler logs: kubectl logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system | tail -n 200
     - Check cloud provider capacity (EC2/Compute Engine spot pool status) and recent scaling events
   - If autoscaler is not scaling: examine cloud account quotas, instance limits, or terraform-managed scaling blocks.
   - Temporary mitigation: scale up a dedicated emergency node pool (runbook command):
     - terraform workspace select prod && terraform apply -target=module.gpu_node_pool -var='name_prefix=inference-urgent' -auto-approve
   - Post-incident: run root cause analysis, update capacity forecasts.

2) P2 - Gradual latency increase / queue backlog
   - Verify whether a model rollout or binary change coincided with the window.
   - Roll back the most recent canary if corroborated by deployment timeline.
   - Increase replicas for the affected service and observe queue metric.

3) P2 - Node replacement flapping (high churn)
   - Check node_boot_time_seconds and instance termination reasons from cloud console.
   - If spot instance eviction driving churn, migrate sensitive pools to on-demand or reserved instances.

Networking and cloud account guardrails

- VPC design: use separate VPC per environment (prod/stage) with shared-service VPC for observability and artifact storage. Use VPC peering or Private Service Connect for regional services.
- Subnet allocation: reserve contiguous /20 blocks per region; document IP allocation matrix in the infra team wiki.
- Egress control: all outbound from inference clusters goes through a NAT gateway or egress proxy to enforce filtering & auditing.
- Service discovery: internal DNS via Route53 private hosted zones; keep zone names consistent: private.inference.<env>.redwood.internal.

Change and release process

- Terraform: PR -> plan -> review -> apply (protected branch gating). For large topology changes (networking, node-type changes): schedule a maintenance window and notify affected teams 72 hours in advance.
- Runtime releases: Canary -> 24h validation period -> gradual ramp -> full promotion. For model changes that affect quality, run the associated eval suite prior to canary.

Operational playbooks / useful commands

- Inspect GPU utilization per node:
  - kubectl exec -it <pod> -c nvml-exporter -- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv
  - kubectl top nodes --use-protocol-buffers
- Check pending pods and scheduling failures:
  - kubectl get pods -n inference --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
  - kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n inference
- Force scale node pool (temporary):
  - aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <asg> --desired-capacity <n>
- Terraform troubleshooting:
  - terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=redwood-terraform-state\"
  - terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars
  - terraform apply -target=module.gpu_node_pool -auto-approve

Postmortem and capacity forecasting cadence

- Capacity forecast: weekly short-term (1-2 weeks) cadence and monthly long-term (6 months) forecast. Include trend lines for model adoption, per-customer reserved capacity, and SLO breach frequency.
- Postmortem policy: for all P1 incidents, complete a blameless postmortem within 7 days with owners and action items tracked in the incident tracker.
